Abstract
Temporal graphs are graphs whose edges are only present at certain points in time. Reachability in
these graphs relies on temporal paths, where edges are traversed chronologically. A temporal graph
that offers all-pairs reachability is said to be temporally connected (or TC). For temporal graphs
that are not TC, a natural question is whether they admit a TC subgraph (a.k.a. closed temporal
component) of a given size k. This question was one of the earliest in the field, shown to be NP-hard
by Bhadra and Ferreira in 2003.
We strengthen this result dramatically, showing that deciding if a TC subgraph exists on at least
3 vertices is already NP-hard in all the standard temporal graph settings (directed/undirected and
strict/non-strict through simple and proper reductions). This implies a strong separation between
closed temporal components and open temporal components (where temporal paths can travel
outside the component), for which inclusion-maximal components can be found in polynomial time.
As a by-product, our reductions strengthen a number of existing results and establish new
derived results. They imply that the size of the largest TC subgraph cannot be approximated within
a factor of (1 −ϵ)n in directed graphs, and within a factor of (1 −ϵ) n
2 in undirected graphs. One of
the reductions also completes the complexity landscape for TC subgraphs of size exactly k when
parameterized by k (answering the missing non-strict case). Finally, on the structural side, our
results imply that there exist arbitrarily large TC graphs of constant lifetime without nontrivial
TC subgraphs, and we also show that there exist TC graphs of arbitrary girth, both facts being of
independent interest.

Introduction
Temporal graphs are graphs whose edges are only present at certain points in time. These
graphs have received significant attention for their ability to model dynamic networks, such
as transportation, communication, social, and robotic networks. Formally, a temporal graph
can be represented by a labeled graph G = (G, λ) where G = (V, E) is a standard finite
graph (directed or undirected) called the underlying graph. The labeling function λ : E →2N
assigns one or several time labels to each edge of E, interpreted as presence times. The largest
time label L is called the lifetime of G. Reachability in these graphs is defined in terms
of paths that traverse the edges chronologically. Precisely, a temporal path is a sequence
⟨(ei, ti)⟩such that ⟨ei⟩is a path in G, ⟨ti⟩is nondecreasing, and ti ∈λ(ei) for all i in the
sequence. The graph G is temporally connected (TC, for short) if it has at least one temporal
path between all ordered pairs of vertices.
Temporal paths differ crucially from standard paths in several aspects. For example,
Kempe, Kleinberg, and Kumar [14] observed that the temporal analog of Menger’s theorem
does not hold: the size of a maximum separator may differ from the maximum number of
internally node-disjoint temporal paths, rendering the problem of finding k node-disjoint
temporal paths between two vertices NP-hard. A further important difference is that temporal
paths are not composable, when the first path ends at a later time step than the second path
starts. Consequently, the reachability relation is nontransitive, with structural and algorithmic
consequences. Bhadra and Ferreira [3] introduced the notion of temporal components—subsets
of vertices that can reach each other by temporal paths. They distinguish between open
components, allowing paths to travel outside the component, and closed components, requiring
that all paths remain inside. In both cases, they observe that, because of the nontransitivity,
(inclusion-wise) maximal temporal components may overlap, and that the component problem
which asks for the existence of a component of a given size k is NP-hard. Interestingly, closed
components correspond to vertex-induced subgraphs that are themselves TC, a quite natural
concept.
The literature on temporal graphs is sensitive to definitional details, whose mention is
unavoidable. Some works consider temporal paths whose time labels are not just required
to be nondecreasing, but strictly increasing, giving rise to so-called strict temporal paths,
connectivity, reachability, and components. Another common distinction is that of simple
versus nonsimple temporal graphs, where simple refers to the fact that every edge is assigned
a single time label. Both distinctions matter, as some of the resulting combinations are
incomparable in terms of expressivity (see e.g. [5] and [10]). For example, it is folklore that
the open and closed versions of the component problem are already NP-hard in the simple
and strict setting, in fact even for lifetime L = 1: for any graph G, the strict temporal
components of the graph G = (G, λ) where λ assigns label 1 to every edge coincide with
the cliques of G. In contrast, the component problem is trivial to solve when L = 1 in
the nonstrict setting, where temporal components coincide with static components. The
above-mentioned reduction from [3] is more subtle and implies that both component problems
are NP-hard also in the nonstrict setting, however considering temporal graphs of lifetime at
least L = 4 and where the edges may have several labels (later strengthened to L = 2 by
Balev, Sanlaville, and Schoeters [1]).
As the reader may feel, the comparison of existing results in temporal graphs is quite
delicate. A convenient way to avoid the distinction between the strict and the nonstrict
settings is to consider proper temporal graphs, where adjacent edges never share a common
label (in directed temporal graphs, this requirement becomes that no in-arc shares a common

label with an out-arc at the same node). For negative results, assuming properness does
not restrict the generality. To the contrary, if a problem is hard when the input is a proper
temporal graph, then de facto, this problem is hard in both the strict and the nonstrict
settings, as no underlying path exists that repeats the same label along two consecutive edges.
Going further, showing that a problem is hard in proper and simple (a.k.a. happy) temporal
graphs establishes at once that it is hard irrespective of the above combinations, making
happy temporal graphs a natural target for reductions. As it happens, open and closed
components are indeed NP-hard in happy temporal graphs [5], although the corresponding
reductions require a nonconstant lifetime.
The systematic study of temporal components from the perspective of parameterized
complexity was initiated in [7], in the nonstrict setting. In that work, Lopes Costa et al.
show that both the open and closed versions of the component problem are W[1]-hard in
the solution size k, as well as in the lifetime L in directed and undirected temporal graphs
(earlier works considered only undirected graphs). In contrast, they show that these two
component problems are FPT when parameterized by the combination k + L in undirected
graphs. They also consider the question of deciding whether a given component is maximal
for inclusion, obtaining an interesting separation: the open version of the component problem
is polynomial-time solvable, while the closed version is hard (in this case, coNP-hard).
Casteigts, Morawietz, and Wolf [6] also considered the parameterized complexity of finding
temporal components, this time in both the strict and the nonstrict setting, in terms of a
new parameter called distance to transitivity, which measures how far the reachability of the
temporal graph is from being transitive. For both settings, they show that deciding if an
open component of size k exists in (un)directed temporal graphs is FPT for this parameter,
whereas the closed version remains NP-hard even when the reachability relation misses a
single pair to be transitive. This negative result is obtained in happy graphs, thus it holds
indistinctively in the strict and the nonstrict settings.
Recently, Deligkas et al. [9] show that both the open and the closed versions of the
problem are NP-hard even when the underlying graph has bounded treewidth, unlike the
case of trees, which is polynomial-time solvable [13]. They also considered a parameter called
temporal path number (namely, the minimum number of temporal paths whose union is the
input graph), for which the open version of the problem is in XP, whereas the closed version
remains NP-hard even for bounded values. Finally, they present FPT algorithms for several
combinations of such parameters. All the results in [9] hold in the strict and the nonstrict
settings, due to counting arguments for positive results, and happy reductions for negative
results.
Further concepts of temporal components have been studied, which are not directly related
to the present work. For example, [1] also investigates round-trip components (providing
reachability plus subsequent return) and recurrent components (realized within all time
windows of a certain duration). Finally, [17] and [2] enumerate components of a slightly
different type, which are either maximal in size or in persistence.
1.1
Contributions
In the above works, the main question is whether a given temporal graph contains a temporal
component of size k or at least k, for given k. Considering the strong connection between
temporal components on the one hand, and cliques in static graphs on the other hand, it
is not surprising that these questions turn out to be hard at least for large values of k. A
natural question is whether this is still the case when k is small, for example a constant value.
Clearly, the problem of deciding if a temporal component of size exactly k exists is tractable

in this case (at least in the XP sense), but is the same true for size at least k? For open
components, both questions are indeed the same, because open components are hereditary
(a fact also observed in [7]), implying that any subset of an open component is an open
component. In contrast, closed components are not hereditary: the existence of a closed
component larger than k does not imply the existence of one of size k. As a consequence, it
is not clear whether the following fundamental question can be solved efficiently:
Nontrivial TC Subgraph:
Input: A temporal graph G.
Question: Does G admit any TC subgraph (a.k.a. closed component) of nontrivial size?
By nontrivial, we mean size at least 2 in the directed case, and size at least 3 in the
undirected case; in other words, any size that requires strictly more than a single edge to be
realized. Our main result is the striking fact that Nontrivial TC Subgraph is indeed
NP-hard, for both directed and undirected temporal graphs even in the happy setting. (For
directed graphs, a happy labeling requires that there is at most one label between every
ordered pair of vertices, and every two composable arcs have different labels.) More precisely,
we obtain the following three main results:
▶Theorem 1.1. Nontrivial TC Subgraph is NP-hard on happy directed temporal graphs
with constant lifetime.
▶Theorem 1.2. Nontrivial TC Subgraph is NP-hard on happy undirected temporal
graphs.
▶Theorem 1.3. Nontrivial TC Subgraph is NP-hard on simple undirected temporal
graphs with constant lifetime in the strict setting.
Note that the two results on undirected temporal graphs are incomparable. Indeed, the
problem cannot be hard for constant lifetime in the happy setting, as an algorithm by Lopes
Costa et al. [7] implies indirectly that Nontrivial TC Subgraph is FPT for the lifetime in
happy undirected graphs (and more generally, in the nonstrict setting). Thus, these results
are tight in terms of the considered setting. These results also strengthen the W[1]-hardness
for k + L by Lopes Costa et al. [7] to a para-NP-hardness for the problem of determining
whether a closed component of size at least k exists (except in the undirected nonstrict
setting, where the problem is FPT). Technically, the presented reductions have further strong
implications for several questions related to closed components. Namely:
1. The reduction for happy undirected temporal graphs answers the open question 4 in [7],
regarding the parameterized complexity of finding closed temporal components of size
exactly k in the nonstrict setting, thereby completing the complexity landscape for
both open or closed components when parameterized by k. For all the other settings,
W[1]-hardness for k is already known, and the fact that our hardness result considers
happy undirected graph implies in particular that it holds in the nonstrict setting.
2. For each setting of the three theorems, determining whether a vertex (in the directed
case) or an edge (in the undirected case) is an inclusion-maximal closed component is
already coNP-hard. This strengthens the result by Lopes Costa et al. [7] that testing
whether a given closed component (of unbounded size) is inclusion-maximal is coNP-hard.
Namely, this problem is already hard when given a component of size 2.
3. Under the Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH), Nontrivial TC Subgraph on happy
directed temporal graphs of constant lifetime or undirected (nonhappy) temporal graphs
of constant lifetime in the strict model cannot be solved in 2o(n) time. In other words, a

1.2
Technical overview
Here, we explain the general ideas behind our reductions. In a sense, all three reductions
follow the same general principle, although the level of technicality increases as the settings
become less expressive. For this reason, the directed case is presented first (in Section 2) and
it can serve as a basis for understanding the more complex undirected cases (described at a
high level in Sections 3 and 4, and with more details in the appendix in Sections C and D).
The following explanations are common to the three reductions.
Each reduction is performed from the NP-hard Multicolored Clique problem, which
is also W[1]-hard for the solution size k [8].
Multicolored Clique (MCC):
Input: An undirected graph G, an integer k, and a k-partition (V1, . . . , Vk) of G such that Vi
(called a color class) is an independent set in G for each i ∈[1, k].
Question: Is there a clique of size k in G?
The vertices V of the MCC instance I become a subset of vertices of the constructed
temporal graph G, which additionally contains two dedicated vertices α and ω and additional
gadgets vertices to ensure temporal reachability between specific vertex pairs of V .
In each reduction, we show that the two vertices α and ω are part of every set of vertices S
that induce a nontrivial TC subgraph. This then implies that G[S] (the subgraph of G induced
by S) has to contain a temporal path from α to ω. We also establish a selection mechanism
that, based on the existence of such a temporal path, ensures that S contains at least one
vertex of each of the color classes Vi of the MCC instance I. By an additional validation
mechanism, we guarantee that vertices of different color classes can be part of the same
TC subgraph only if they are adjacent in the MCC instance. This validation mechanism is
achieved by introducing additional vertices Vcon. The main difficulty now is that adjacent
vertices from the MCC instance must reach all vertices of the connector gadget Vcon associated
with them and conversely, these vertices of the connector gadget must reach the respective
vertices of the MCC instance. However, this must be done in a way that avoids that the two
clique vertices plus their associated vertices of the connector gadget already form a closed
tcc. This construction guarantees that a nontrivial TC subgraph in G implies the existence
of a clique of size k in I.
For the other direction, we show that a clique X of size k in I implies a nontrivial TC
subgraph in G. To this end, we show that X ∪Vcon ∪{α, ω} induces a nontrivial TC subgraph.
Intuitively, the temporal connectivity is ensured as follows: all vertices of Vcon can reach α
early, then follow paths from α to all vertices of X ∪{ω}, and finally reach each vertex

◀
The implications.
Implication 2 for this setting follows by the fact that in the family of
constructed instances by these reductions, α is part of every closed tcc of size at least 2.
Hence, it is coNP-hard to decide whether the set {α} is an inclusion-maximal closed tcc.
Next, Implication 3 for this setting follows due to the fact that in the reduction, the
number of vertices n in G is O(|V |). An algorithm to solve Nontrivial TC Subgraph on
happy directed temporal graphs that runs in 2o(n) time would imply an algorithm for MCC
that runs in 2o(|V |) time. The latter, however, is not possible if the ETH is true [12].
Finally, Implication 4 for this setting can be obtained by slightly extending the reduction.
For each fixed 0 < ϵ < 1, we can add vertices q to the connector gadget with arc (ω, q) with
label 10 and arc (q, α) with label 2, until the size of the connector gadget is at least (1−ϵ)|V ∗|
where V ∗is the vertex set of the current graph. The resulting temporal graph then has a
nontrivial closed tcc if and only if the original graph had one. As we showed, the connector
gadget is part of every maximal nontrivial closed tcc, just due to the arcs incident with α
and ω. Hence, the resulting temporal graph has a TC subgraph of size at least (1 −ϵ)n if
and only if it has a nontrivial TC subgraph. This implies that it is NP-hard to distinguish

Structural Analysis and Gadgets for the Undirected Case
In this section, we prepare the gadget for the undirected case. A simple adaptation of
the directed reduction is not possible. In fact, if we would make each arc in the previous
reduction undirected, we would immediately get triangles2 in the underlying graph, which
would be a sufficient condition for the existence of closed tcc of nontrivial size, that is, of
size 3. Hence, to obtain a gadget for the undirected case that mimics the behavior of the
directed connectivity gadget, we aim to replace each vertex inx and outy by a constant size
temporal graph P that contains no nontrivial closed tcc. This in particular implies that P
must be triangle-free. Moreover, as the vertices of such a gadget P need to reach α early
and ω needs to reach all vertices of P late, P also needs two disjoint spanning trees (assuming
that only one vertex of P will be connected to α and only one vertex of P will be connected
to ω). In our first subsection, we show that TC graphs with these properties exist. In fact,
we show the existence of TC graph of arbitrary girth and where additionally both spanning
trees are Hamiltonian paths. We will then modify the labeling of one such a graph to obtain
our gadget. The property that the spanning trees are Hamiltonian paths will be helpful to

Conclusion
In this paper, we significantly refined the lower bounds for finding TC subgraphs (closed
temporally connected components) in a given temporal graph. We showed that even when
asking for components of size at least 2 in the directed case and size at least 3 in the


Arnaud Casteigts, Christian Komusiewicz, Nils Morawietz
13
undirected case, the task can presumably not be performed in polynomial time. Restricting
the temporal graphs to have a constant lifetime does not change the complexity here, except
in the case of undirected temporal graphs with nonstrict reachability. Our reductions imply a
number of significant side results; in particular, they answer the open question [7] of whether
finding a TC subgraph of size exactly k in the nonstrict model on undirected temporal graphs
can be done in FPT time for k.
Following this work, there are a number of natural directions for future work:
We show that determining the existence of a nontrivial TC subgraph in the nonstrict
model on undirected temporal graphs can not be solved in 2o(√n) time. The trivial upper
bound is at 2O(n) time. Is it possible to improve the upper-bound to 2O(√n) time?
Our work essentially only considers lower bounds. It would be interesting to see for
which parameters the problem can be solved in FPT time. For example, is it possible
to solve the problem in FPT time for the treewidth of the underlying graph? In recent
work [9], it was shown that finding a large TC subgraph is NP-hard even on graphs of
bounded treewidth, but the presented reduction is guaranteed to contain small nontrivial
TC subgraphs.
It would also be interesting to consider further models of components, for example the
closed version of the round-trip components in [1], or closed components that are not
completely TC, but still highly connected, for example where half of the vertices can
reach each other by temporal paths. These property seem to share with TC subgraphs
the feature that they are neither hereditary nor quasi-hereditary, making their study an
interesting target for future works.

Abstract: Temporal graphs are graphs whose edges are only present at certain points in time. Reachability in these graphs relies on temporal paths, where edges are traversed chronologically. A temporal graph that offers all-pairs reachability is said to be temporally connected (or TC). For temporal graphs that are not TC, a natural question is whether they admit a TC subgraph (a.k.a. closed temporal component) of a given size k. This question was one of the earliest in the field, shown to be NP-hard by Bhadra and Ferreira in 2003. We strengthen this result dramatically, showing that deciding if a TC subgraph exists on at least 3 vertices is already NP-hard in all the standard temporal graph settings (directed/undirected and strict/non-strict through simple and proper reductions). This implies a strong separation between closed temporal components and open temporal components (where temporal paths can travel outside the component), for which inclusion-maximal components can be found in polynomial time. As a by-product, our reductions strengthen a number of existing results and establish new derived results. They imply that the size of the largest TC subgraph cannot be approximated within a factor of (1 −ϵ)n in directed graphs, and within a factor of (1 −ϵ) n 2 in undirected graphs. One of the reductions also completes the complexity landscape for TC subgraphs of size exactly k when parameterized by k (answering the missing non-strict case). Finally, on the structural side, our results imply that there exist arbitrarily large TC graphs of constant lifetime without nontrivial TC subgraphs, and we also show that there exist TC graphs of arbitrary girth, both facts being of independent interest. 2012 ACM Subject Classification Theory of computation →Graph algorithms analysis; Mathematics of computing →Discrete mathematics
